props.title: All That Jazz
props.initialSlug: A director's dazzling dance with death and showbiz

sections.content: All That Jazz (1979) revolutionized the movie musical through its raw, autobiographical lens into show business self-destruction. Director Bob Fosse essentially filmed his own death, casting Roy Scheider as Joe Gideon, a chain-smoking, pill-popping choreographer pushing himself to the brink. The film's influence echoes through later showbiz stories like Black Swan (2010) and Birdman (2014), but none match its hallucinatory blend of dance numbers and hospital scenes. Like Federico Fellini's 8½ (1963), it's a master artist turning his own creative crisis into boundary-pushing cinema.

sections.content: The film's structure is genius - intercutting Gideon's real-world collapse with fantasy sequences where he confronts Angelique (Jessica Lange), a glamorous Angel of Death. These surreal interludes influenced countless films, from Requiem for a Dream (2000) to I'm Thinking of Ending Things (2020). The legendary "Bye Bye Life" finale, where Gideon performs his own death, remains one of cinema's most audacious sequences.

What sets All That Jazz apart is its technical mastery of both musical numbers and psychological drama. The opening audition sequence set to "On Broadway" established a template for showing the brutal reality of dancer life that influenced Center Stage (2000) and Whiplash (2014). Editor Alan Heim's Oscar-winning cutting creates a rhythm that makes Gideon's downward spiral feel like a dark dance itself. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

sections.content: The film's DNA appears everywhere in modern entertainment storytelling. Fosse/Verdon (2019) directly dramatized its making, while shows like Bojack Horseman (2014-2020) echo its brutal honesty about entertainment industry self-destruction. Even The Weeknd's "Blinding Lights" music video pays homage to the film's hospital hallucination sequences.
